items.title: Frank Turek Fights ‘War on Reality,’ Offers Warning for America
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "Dystopia"
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Apologist Frank Turek is on a mission to tackle the “war on reality,” warning Americans face a “dystopia” if the nation continues marching toward Marxism.

Turek’s new book, “The War on Reality Workbook: Recovering Truth in a World That Celebrates Lies,” is being released as the nation recently remembered the one-year anniversary of the assassination of conservative and Christian commentator Charlie Kirk.

The apologist told CBN News he and his coauthor, Phoenix Hayes, dedicated the book to Kirk, calling the late Turning Point USA founder a “warrior for reality.”

Turek broke down the current state of culture and decried many elements that simply make no logical — or biblical — sense.

“Abortion is healthcare; we’re pulling baby body parts out of women, and we’re calling that health care,” he said. “That’s a war on reality, and Charlie was a casualty in the war on reality. But, thankfully, since he was a believer, all the murderer was able to do is change his address.”

Turek continued, “He’s absent from the body, present with the Lord, and we remain behind, still engaged in fighting for reality when so many forces are fighting against.”

items.title: Christian Singer Colton Dixon Says Charlie Kirk’s Assassination ‘Changed’ Him
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "It gave me a new outlook on things."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Christian singer-songwriter Colton Dixon said the assassination of Charlie Kirk and the government’s restrictive response to the COVID-19 pandemic “changed” him.

Dixon, 35, told CBN News seeing Kirk murdered for exercising his right to free speech pushed him “to seek truth harder.”

“I feel like, just for a lot of people, whether you believed in what Charlie stood for or not, just for a lot of people, it was, like, it just — I don’t know, it changed me,” said Dixon. “It was just, like, ‘Wow.’ [It] gave me a new outlook on things, even just to seek truth harder.”

The up-and-coming generation, he added, aren’t taking things at face-value anymore, regardless of the source. “They’re seeking truth for themselves,” he explained.

As a Christian recording artist, Dixon said he believes he has found the answer: “The answer’s Jesus.”

The recent spate of culture-defining events have, according to the “Build a Boat” singer, “anchored my feet down in my beliefs so that I’m not going to be pushed around by a little Chihuahua who might bark louder.”

“I kind of even really figured out why I believe what I believe,” he said. “[B]ecause again, it’s just COVID and just all these different things, they’re trying to get you to do different things and I’m like, ‘OK, why aren’t we just going to do it?’ Let’s figure out why so we’re not just being stubborn [and] hardheaded.”

“We open up God’s Word, we pray, we seek godly wisdom, and then we come to the conclusion, ‘Oh, this is why,'” Dixon said. “So now I just feel more steadfast in why I believe what I believe.”

As he’s ruminated on his convictions in recent years, Dixon has become noticeably more comfortable creating edgier content — at least edgier for the status quo in the contemporary Christian music world.

The “American Idol” alumnus just released a new song, “Bones,” based on the Old Testament passage of Ezekiel 37, chronicling the story of the prophet being transported to a valley filled with dry bones. God asked whether the bones could live and then commanded Ezekiel to prophesy over them. As the prophet began speaking promises to the bones, they assembled and were covered in flesh. Then a second prophecy called breath to fill their lungs and they became a living army standing to their feet.

Dixon said the song is “straight from Scripture,” recalling reading the biblical account and feeling “super inspired” and “like God gave me revelation” about speaking “over the dead things in your life.”

During a time of year when most of American culture is fixated on death from a secular perspective, Dixon saw an opportunity to flip the script around Halloween with a biblical understanding of death.

“What if we could … take this passage that already theatrically lines up with a lot of the visuals of skeletons — that’s what this whole passage was, it was a valley of dry bones, the bones rattling, coming together, flesh coming upon the bones, it was like zombies out there, you know, in Ezekiel 37,” he reflected.

That passage of Scripture, Dixon emphasized, shows a biblical interpretation of death, which, for the Christian, he said, is “just a little blip on the timeline of what our lives look like.”

He said, “For the rest of the world, death is the final word. … That’s the period. Life after death is this big mystery. But for a believer, death is not the final word; the cross —what Jesus did on the cross — is the final word, and not only that, but three days later, Him resurrecting from the grave so that we could spend eternal life with Him in heaven. … Death can be a scary thing to talk about, but as a believer, I don’t think it should be.”

The song — and its music video, which is set at night in a graveyard — is certainly unorthodox in its approach, but it paints a clear picture to the world that this life is not all there is. It also tells the story of spiritual power, a nod toward Romans 8:11, where Paul wrote, “The Spirit of God, who raised Jesus from the dead, lives in you. And just as God raised Christ Jesus from the dead, he will give life to your mortal bodies by this same Spirit living within you” (NLT).

“I think that this song is … a kick in the pants for sideline Christians, where I’ve found myself before,” said Dixon. “It’s time to start using the spiritual authority that we have as believers and not just talk the talk, but walk it, as well.”

In fact, for Dixon, it was his wife Annie’s certainty about spiritual authority that led him to do some self-reflection.

“I found myself being so in awe of [my wife] that that was her first response [to pray and speak over things],” he said. “But then also going, ‘Why isn’t that mine?’ You know? If I’m really going to be the best spiritual leader of our house, I need to stop kicking my feet up and actually get in the game and start doing this for real.”

items.title: This Sunday, the Global Church Will Pray for 388 Million Christians Facing High Levels of Persecution
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: Congregations around the world will set aside Sunday, Nov. 1 for the International Day of Prayer for the Persecuted Church, and this year Open Doors, the Christian ministry that tracks persecution, is asking them to start with Syria. Its 2026 World Watch List moved Syria from 18th place to sixth, a
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Congregations around the world will set aside Sunday, Nov. 1 for the International Day of Prayer for the Persecuted Church, and this year Open Doors, the Christian ministry that tracks persecution, is asking them to start with Syria.

Its 2026 World Watch List moved Syria from 18th place to sixth, a 12-point jump in its score and the largest in the top 10. Open Doors says Syria is now at its most dangerous for Christians since the Islamic State group occupied significant parts of the country.

About 300,000 Christians live in Syria. Since the fall of the Assad government in December 2024, the country has been mostly controlled by forces led by Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham, an Islamic extremist group with roots in al-Qaeda. The group has made overtures toward moderation and held talks with representatives of Syria’s traditional Christian communities, but it is too soon to know what will come of the new leadership. Widespread instability has produced deadly clashes that have affected Druze and Alawites in particular, with Christians caught in the crossfire, and Islamic State attacks have resumed, including the deadly attack on a church in Damascus in June 2025.

“The trauma of what happened hit us all hard,” said “Mourad,” who is responsible for the work of Open Doors’ local partner in Syria. “We thought getting rid of the previous regime would give us some sense of freedom, yet it seems there are still people who only believe in killing.”

The interim Syrian constitution adopted in March 2025 makes Islamic law the main source of legislation, and it offers insufficient protection for religious minorities. Pressure on Christians is greatest in Damascus and Aleppo, while the northeast is generally safer.

The World Watch List ranks the 50 countries where Christians face the most extreme persecution, using a points system built on data from experts on the ground in 100 countries. North Korea is first with a score of 97 out of 100, followed by Somalia, Yemen, Sudan and Eritrea. Syria is sixth with 90, ahead of Nigeria, Pakistan, Libya and Iran. Open Doors counts more than 388 million Christians worldwide facing high levels of persecution and discrimination for their faith, about one in seven, and in the top 50 countries alone, more than 315 million face very high or extreme persecution. In its 2026 report it recorded 4,849 Christians killed, 4,712 detained and 3,632 churches and Christian properties attacked.

For more than 1,600 years Christians have set aside early November to remember believers who suffered for their faith. Open Doors’ free toolkit for churches and small groups includes guided prayer points, videos, sermon material and social images, and this year’s focus is the Middle East, beginning with Syria.

Open Doors’ prayer points for Syria ask for three things: that believers would lean on God as their “Rock eternal” (Isaiah 26:4), that converts from Islam would find love and fellowship even when family and friends reject them, and that the victims of the Damascus church attack would feel God’s closeness.

items.title: Sunday, November 1, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, today we celebrate the Solemnity of All Saints. Many who have stood in the presence of the Gothic rose windows—brightly fashioned with images of the saints—have heard the windows sing.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Revelation 7:2-4, 9-14

I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, having the seal of the living God, and he called with a loud voice to the four angels who had been given power to damage earth and sea, saying, “Do not damage the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have marked the servants of our God with a seal on their foreheads.”

And I heard the number of those who were sealed, one hundred forty-four thousand, sealed out of every tribe of the people of Israel:

After this I looked, and there was a great multitude that no one could count, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, robed in white, with palm branches in their hands. They cried out in a loud voice, saying,

“Salvation belongs to our God who is seated on the throne, and to the Lamb!”

And all the angels stood around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God, singing,

“Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom
and thanksgiving and honor
and power and might
be to our God forever and ever! Amen.”

Then one of the elders addressed me, saying, “Who are these, robed in white, and where have they come from?” I said to him, “Sir, you are the one that knows.” Then he said to me, “These are they who have come out of the great ordeal; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

Psalm
Psalm 24:1bc-2, 3-4ab, 5-6

The earth is the Lord’s and all that is in it,
    the world, and those who live in it;
for he has founded it on the seas,
    and established it on the rivers.
Who shall ascend the hill of the Lord?
    And who shall stand in his holy place?
Those who have clean hands and pure hearts,
    who do not lift up their souls to what is false,
    and do not swear deceitfully.
They will receive blessing from the Lord,
    and vindication from the God of their salvation.
Such is the company of those who seek him,
    who seek the face of the God of Jacob. Selah

Second Reading
1 John 3:1-3

See what love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God; and that is what we are. The reason the world does not know us is that it did not know him. Beloved, we are God’s children now; what we will be has not yet been revealed. What we do know is this: when he is revealed, we will be like him, for we will see him as he is. And all who have this hope in him purify themselves, just as he is pure.

Gospel Reading
Matthew 5:1-12a

When Jesus saw the crowds, he went up the mountain; and after he sat down, his disciples came to him. Then he began to speak, and taught them, saying:

“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

“Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.

“Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth.

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled.

“Blessed are the merciful, for they will receive mercy.

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.

“Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

“Blessed are you when people revile you and persecute you and utter all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven, for in the same way they persecuted the prophets who were before you.

Reflection

Friends, today we celebrate the Solemnity of All Saints. Many who have stood in the presence of the Gothic rose windows—brightly fashioned with images of the saints—have heard the windows sing. The Lord Jesus says, “For whoever wishes to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it” (Matt 16:25), and this wonderful loss of self happens when we listen to the singing of the rose window.

The rose is also an evocative symbol of what the spiritual masters refer to as the center. At the center is a depiction of Christ. Then wheeling around the Christic core is a harmoniously arranged amalgam of “medallions,” images, from the lives of the saints.

The medallions are often connected to one another and to the center by a series of spokes. This structured harmony is intended to be a picture of the well-ordered soul. When the divine power is the uncompromised center of our lives—as it is for the saints—then the myriad energies of our souls—intellectual, moral, physical, emotional, sexual—tend to fall into harmony around it. 

When Christ is the “ground” of the soul, the soul finds peace, order, and beauty. Make God’s will the center of your concerns, and your proximate needs, desires, and longings will tend to find their place.

items.title: ‘Defend Us From Evil’: Lessons from the Inklings
items.author: Henry T. Edmondson III
items.summary:
Henry T. Edmondson III

What better opportunity than the end of October to visit or revisit several of the Inklings' publications to see what they might tell us about spiritual malevolence?
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Henry T. Edmondson III

The house down the street is decorated with an array of tombstones of different shapes and sizes strewn across the front yard. Strings of purple lights hang across the roof. It’s all been there for about three months in preparation for the family’s favorite—and apparently only—religious holiday, Halloween. Drive around the city but take care of giant spiders, zombies, reawakened corpses, skeletons, and Grim Reapers. All Hallows’ Eve has been commercialized into oblivion, thus illustrating the Christian concept that evil has no substance of its own; rather, it is a perversion of what is good. Although it may be all in good fun, such gory paraphernalia dismiss the reality of evil by treating it flippantly.

In the first half of the twentieth century, based at Oxford University and occasionally meeting at the Eagle and the Child pub, were one of history’s most productive friendships. This group, the Inklings, have played an astonishing role in explaining and defending, through prose and fiction, the Christian life. What better opportunity than the end of October to visit or revisit several of their publications to see what they might tell us about spiritual malevolence? The Inklings offer no systematic teaching on the issue, and it is beyond the scope of this essay to try to draw a comprehensive theology from their writing. It is within reach, however, to tease out vital principles on spiritual warfare that are essential in these perilous times. They did not always agree, but even the tensions between their respective contributions are instructive.

Charles Williams: “We Wrestle Not Against Flesh and Blood”

The core members of the Inklings were C. S. Lewis, J. R. R. Tolkien, Charles Williams, and Owen Barfield. In his upcoming book Tolkien and the Inklings: Men of the West, scholar Bradley J. Birzer notes that among the four, Williams may have done the most to sharpen his fellow Inklings’ sense of evil, especially C. S. Lewis, although Tolkien’s contributions may be the most elegant and far‑reaching. 

If C. S. Lewis’s personality sometimes left his colleagues off balance, neither is Charles Williams easily understood, especially given his interest in the occult. Williams’s excursions to the dark side, though—risky as they were—may have enabled him to bring to his colleagues a keen awareness of the spiritual backdrop of everyday life. Granted, Williams’s fiction is an acquired taste, and some may not find it to their liking. His talent, though, lies in impressing upon the reader that, as the Apostle explains, “our struggle is not against enemies of blood and flesh” (Eph 6:12). 

Williams’s first published novel, War in Heaven, as the title implies, is a contest between good and evil, involving interaction between everyday life and the timeless spiritual world in which a priest struggles against a satanic cabal. C. S. Lewis called War in Heaven a “spiritual shocker.” All Hallows’ Eve involves a foul mystic, “Simon the Clerk,” who while advancing toward his “spiritual enthronement” is successfully opposed by Lester. Recently deceased, Lester has limited interaction with the living, including her living husband, Richard. For his part, Richard perceives “a breach of spiritual law” that produces an awareness of something “so full of vileness that he almost fainted.” In a perversion of the Holy Trinity, Simon is tripartite as he exists in three different locations. In Williams’s book The Place of the Lion, a rift has occurred in the barrier between the natural and the supernatural, allowing an invasion of malicious entities who must be beaten back by benevolent forces.

C. S. Lewis: Temptation and Truth

C. S. Lewis’s novel That Hideous Strength, the third of his “Space Trilogy,” was deeply influenced by Williams. Indeed, it employs the same theme of life transpiring against a backdrop of good and evil forces. Truth and humility are potent forces of good in the fight against evil.

Lewis’s The Screwtape Letters reminds us that devious temptation lurks around every corner. In the first letter in the collection of thirty-one letters between Screwtape and his nephew Wormwood, the elder demon explains the best strategy against a human being is to keep him ignorant of the very existence of the demonic.

Whereas That Hideous Strength involves the supernatural, The Screwtape Letters is more mundane, as long as you can imagine letters between an avuncular demon and his protégé. (It may be easier to think of email or texting.) In “Letter 6,” Screwtape advises Wormwood to urge the “patient” to constantly fret about the future rather than focus on the present. “Letter 14” reveals that the human virtue that the scheming devils fear most is humility.

Although it might not seem so, Lewis greatest contribution to spiritual warfare may be The Abolition of Man. Using the Tao (from the ancient Chinese philosophy and religion of Taoism) as a symbol of the universal timeless character of truth, the book is a refutation of relativism. The book develops, Lewis writes, “the doctrine of objective value, the belief that certain attitudes are really true, and others really false.”

Objective certainty is the foundation of the religious life—or simply a good life. Yet the modern spread of cultural relativism denies the existence of good and evil. Some lament that we live in a post-truth society in which truth is good only insofar as it serves an immediate purpose. Lewis makes an important connection; namely, that personal character rests on objective truth. Otherwise, what does courage defend, and why is honor given? Of what does wisdom consist? And where are the principles upon which Prudence draws to make difficult decisions? Lewis famously observes,

In a sort of ghastly simplicity we remove the organ and demand the function. We make men without chests and expect of them virtue and enterprise. We laugh at honour and are shocked to find traitors in our midst. We castrate and bid the geldings be fruitful.

Notably, in The Abolition of Man, it is higher education that Lewis holds responsible for “de-bunking” the inherited wisdom that students may bring to the classroom that only makes them vulnerable to propaganda. A better explanation of higher education today would be hard to find: witless college students engage in protests-cum-riots about issues they barely understand.

The task of the modern educator is not to cut down jungles but to irrigate deserts. The right defence against false sentiments is to inculcate just sentiments. By starving the sensibility of our pupils we only make them easier prey to the propagandist when he comes. 

Tolkien: The Ebb and Flow of Evil 

The Lord of the Rings is shot through with unambiguous references to evil; to be sure, the quest of the Fellowship is to destroy Sauron’s greatest weapon. In LOTR, Tolkien is not merely addressing “evil men” or “evil deeds,” but “evil,” having an identity of its own; he employs “evil” as a noun, not only as an adjective.

The author sets the tone early in the saga:

It seemed that the evil power in Mirkwood had been driven out . . . only to reappear in greater strength in the old strongholds of Mordor. The Dark Tower had been rebuilt, it was said. From there the power was spreading far and wide, and away far east and south there were wars and growing fear. Orcs were multiplying again in the mountains. Trolls were abroad, no longer dull-witted, but cunning and armed with dreadful weapons. And there were murmured hints of creatures more terrible than all these, but they had no name.

Aragorn warns, “There is evil afoot . . . and the West is no longer safe.” The fight, moreover, is ongoing, as Aragorn explains, “Other evils there are that may come; for Sauron is himself but a servant or emissary. . . . Hardly has our strength sufficed to beat off the first great assault. The next will be greater.”

Aragorn thus warns of a kind of dynamic ebb and flow of evil among men and women. Arguably, at this moment in history, we are witnessing a flow. The tide, moreover, is still coming in. We fear to ask what the high tide will bring.

Finally, Tolkien asserts that the fight against evil is undertaken with different spheres of responsibility. The Screwtape Letters concerned Tolkien because he thought his companion should keep a healthy distance from the study of the demonic; at best, such inquiries should be carried out by those with the proper training, and in some cases, ordination. Flannery O’Connor echoed Tolkien’s warning when she wrote that for most of us, “A working knowledge of the devil can be very well had from resisting him.”

This chain of command, so to speak, is also illustrated by the “palantíri”: think of it as a Middle Earth Facetime call. Alternatively called the “Seeing Stones,” they show real objects or events, but they may do so selectively. The stones enable individuals to see one another and communicate—but only those of a “great strength of will” dare to use them, and even then, they might do so at their peril. What was shown, moreover, could be more important than what was selectively presented. In LOTR, a palantír has fallen into the enemy’s hands (Sauron), making the use of all other existing stones hazardous. Denethor, steward king of Gondor, has another stone, and it drives him to self-immolation. The hobbit Pippin’s life is put in peril when he sneaks a look through a palantír, but Gandalf saves him from destruction.

Yet later, Gandalf announces that Aragorn, the “Returning King,” would keep the palantír as it would facilitate his reign over Middle-earth “to see what is passing in his realm, and what his servants are doing.” It seems that we ordinary hobbits should leave the palantíri to those who are better equipped for its use.

“St. Michael the Archangel, Defend Us in Battle”

It has become commonplace for priests and the congregation to recite the prayer to St. Michael after Mass. It started on October 1, 1884, when Pope Leo XIII experienced a vision of demonic forces attacking the Church. Immediately after Mass, he went to his office and penned the original, longer version of the prayer to St. Michael and mandated it be recited by priests and the congregation after every Low Mass. The practice fell into disuse after Vatican II, but in his Regina Coeli address on April 24, 1994, thirty years after Leo XIII introduced the prayer, Pope John Paul II revived the use of the prayer. He said, “I ask everyone not to forget it, and to recite it to obtain help in the battle against the forces of darkness and against the spirit of the world.”

The regular recitation of any prayer can become perfunctory, so it may be useful to recite the longer original version of the prayer once a week or so. The shortened version consists of fifty-nine words, but the original prayer spans 606 words, making it hard to skip through while distracted by the fourth-grader’s low math score or yesterday’s triple bogey on the fourteenth hole. The first and last paragraphs may whet your appetite: 

O Glorious Prince of the heavenly host, St. Michael the Archangel, defend us in the battle and in the terrible warfare that we are waging against the principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world of darkness, against the evil spirits. Come to the aid of man, whom Almighty God created immortal, made in His own image and likeness, and redeemed at a great price from the tyranny of Satan.

[ . . .]

Let us pray. O God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, we call upon Thy holy Name, and as supplicants, we implore Thy clemency, that by the intercession of Mary, ever Virgin Immaculate and our Mother, and of the glorious St. Michael the Archangel, Thou wouldst deign to help us against Satan and all the other unclean spirits who wander about the world for the injury of the human race and the ruin of souls. Amen.
